feat(topology): rebuild the universe topology ingest as a queue chain

Fills stars, planets, moons, asteroid_belts, stargates and stations from
ESI through a queue chain in which every table has exactly one writer.

worker-solar-systems used to fill six tables inside a single large
transaction. It now writes solar_systems alone and publishes to four
downstream queues. worker-planets is the chain node: it writes planets
and publishes the moon and asteroid belt messages, carrying the
moon-to-planet link that /universe/moons/{id}/ does not return and that
nothing else can recover. The rest are leaves owning one table each.

The schema enforces what it can. Moons and asteroid belts reach their
planet through a composite (planet_id, solar_system_id) foreign key, so a
moon can no longer belong to a planet in another system. On stargates,
destination_system_id is ON DELETE SET NULL rather than cascade: deleting
a system must empty the destinations of gates in other systems, not
delete those gates. destination_stargate_id deliberately has no foreign
key, because the same worker writes both ends and a constraint would turn
an ordering detail inside one queue into a hard failure. Indexes are
aligned with the queries the resolvers actually run.

The migration is hand written. prisma migrate diff wanted to drop
killmail_filters, character_kill_stats, corporation_kill_stats,
alliance_kill_stats and refresh_log - 99,724 rows in tables that live
outside prisma/schema by design - and those statements were removed
before applying it with migrate deploy.

The queue scripts stop being scans and become repair tools. queue:stars
and its siblings read their own WHERE name IS NULL rows and republish
only those, which for celestials ESI exposes by ID alone is the only
possible source of truth. yarn doctor:topology reports what the schema
cannot: orphaned cross-pipeline references, unnamed rows per table with
the repair command for each, and dead letter depth.

Workers now end on their own, once the queue has been quiet for an idle
window and nothing is still in flight. Both conditions are needed: with a
prefetch above 1 the queue drains while messages are still being
processed, and closing the channel then would requeue them with their
rows unwritten. Exit status is 1 if the run had errors. Against an
already empty queue a worker says so and exits instead of hanging.
SIGTERM now shuts one down as gracefully as SIGINT already did.

Per-row results are logged at info with a [n] counter and a progress
summary every 100 rows, following the worker-info-* family. Production
workers do keep log records - PM2 captures the console transport into
out_file for every app - so a result line that exists only at debug is
dropped by each one configured at info. The batch line in
queue-solar-systems.ts goes the other way, back to debug, matching
queue-regions and queue-constellations, the two root scans it is a
sibling of, and 16 of the 19 queue scripts that have such a line.

ESI_MAX_RPS and ESI_PREFETCH replace the hardcoded rate ceiling and
prefetch. The rate defaults reproduce the previous numbers exactly -
50/sec, a 20 ms dispatch gap, 50 concurrent - so nothing changes unless a
knob is turned. The ceiling is per process, which is what makes two
workers 100 req/sec rather than 50.

Verified by a full ingest: solar_systems 8,490, stars 8,089, planets
68,407, stargates 13,978 with every destination resolved, stations 5,210,
asteroid_belts 40,928, moons 344,457. doctor:topology reports no unnamed
rows, no orphans and an empty dead letter queue; the only non-zero count
is stations.owner_corporation_id, which points at corporations the
corporation pipeline has not fetched.

Documented in backend/docs/workers/universe-topology-chain.md and the
runbook at backend/docs/ops/universe-topology-run.md. CLAUDE.md's rate
limiting section is corrected for worker-solar-systems, which no longer
belongs with the prefetch(1) workers.

fix(awareness): a working module reported broken for three months, by one codec (#2004)

* fix(awareness): a working module reported broken for three months, by one codec

`health_prober._probe_module_import` is the cheap stand-in for
`python -c "import <module>"` -- its own docstring says so, because spawning
842 subprocesses would take forever. It read the source with

    abs_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")

and plain utf-8 leaves a leading BYTE ORDER MARK in the string as U+FEFF.
`ast.parse` then rejects it: "invalid non-printable character U+FEFF ...
line 1".

PYTHON'S REAL IMPORT MACHINERY TOLERATES A LEADING BOM. So every one of these
files imports perfectly from a shell, and the probe was answering a different
question from the one it claims to.

MEASURED ON THE LIVE BOARD 2026-09-01:
  * FOUR files carry a BOM -- tools/network/bgp_predictor.py,
    tools/network/capacity_predictor.py, tools/network/supply_chain_risk.py and
    tools/databridge/connectors/skillhub_connector.py. ALL FOUR IMPORT; each was
    verified with `python -c "import ..."` before this was written.
  * 421 recorded `fail` snapshots carrying this error, on EVERY probe run since
    2026-06-14 -- about three months of a daily false alarm.
  * The 2-probe confirmation rule cannot catch it. That rule exists to filter
    TRANSIENT failures; this one is perfectly reproducible, so it confirmed to
    `fail` every time and kept filing kanban cards.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, which is the part worth keeping. The scheduled card
`[Batch] module_import: 471 regression findings to address` reads as a
platform-wide emergency. Splitting the 1,170 current failures by CAUSE gives a
different picture entirely:
    1,164  "file not found"  -- stale index nodes for files deliberately
                                deleted when the trading domain left for the
                                private ICDEV[FT] repo. ZERO of them exist on
                                disk, so the index is simply behind; the
                                indexer already has a sweep for that.
        6  U+FEFF            -- this, all one file, and a real defect.
A count of 471 findings was one genuine bug wearing 471 hats.

THE FIX IS THE CODEC. `utf-8-sig` strips a leading BOM and is otherwise
identical to utf-8, so the probe now reads a file the way the import system
does. It strips ONLY a leading mark: a U+FEFF in the BODY is a real defect --
what a bad editor write leaves behind -- and the importer rejects that too, so
the probe must keep surfacing it. A test pins exactly that, and another pins
that a genuinely broken file still raises, so this cannot decay into "ignore
syntax errors". `errors="replace"` is kept: a sweep over 842 files must not die
on one unreadable byte.

The fix is pinned AT ITS CAUSE -- a test asserts the reader uses `utf-8-sig` --
because a test that only checked the outcome would pass again the moment
somebody "fixed" it by catching the SyntaxError instead.

NOT WIDENED, and named rather than left silent: `tools/ace/agent_tools.py`,
`tools/ace/controller.py` and `tools/ace/role_loader.py` also pair
`read_text(encoding="utf-8")` with a parse and may carry the same defect. They
are a different surface with different inputs and deserve their own
investigation and tests, not a drive-by edit here.

THE SKIP CENSUS CAUGHT MY OWN FIRST DRAFT, and it was right. That draft named
the four files and skipped when one was absent; the pre-commit gate refused it
-- "a skipped test satisfies the coverage claim while asserting nothing" -- so
the test now DISCOVERS the files carrying a BOM instead of listing them, and
there is no skip to register. A defensive skip about tracked, stable files was
an excuse, not a safeguard.

8 tests, red first. Gated in args/ci_test_files/core.d/. 340 awareness tests
pass. ruff clean. No migration.

Kubernetes, read-only — and give the monitor a shape that survives six modules

## The UX problem, which was mine and which I created incrementally

Every module built today appended a panel to the Fleet Monitor. Each one
looked reasonable on its own. The composite did not: with all modules on,
the page opened with FIVE stacked forms — search, a command box, a log
tailer, a cron reader, a container list — above the health summary and the
server cards. The thing the page is named for sat below four tools nobody
was using at that moment.

The monitor now has sub-navigation: Overview plus one tab per enabled
module. Overview is the default and holds what the page is for.

Panels stay MOUNTED and are hidden rather than unmounted. A running
broadcast or an open log tail has to survive a glance at the overview — and
LogTailPanel stops its remote command on unmount, so unmounting on tab
switch would kill a tail mid-read. A module switched off while its tab is
open falls back to Overview rather than leaving a blank page.

## Kubernetes

The roadmap says doing this badly is worse than not doing it, so the file
states where the line is rather than leaving it to be discovered:

- No context switching. `kubectl config use-context` rewrites the user's
  kubeconfig for every process on that host. A tool that repoints someone's
  cluster because they used a dropdown is how a manifest reaches prod
  believing it is staging. Context is passed per read with `--context`.
- No exec. That is `docker exec` with more blast radius and a separate RBAC
  story; it belongs behind broadcast's approval model, not a button beside
  a pod name.
- Nothing that writes.

RBAC is what makes this different from Docker, and it is handled as data
rather than as an error: `--all-namespaces` is the common denial, so pods
fall back to the current namespace and the result records WHICH happened —
an empty list means something different depending on it, and the panel says
so. Six failure classes, each with its own remedy: forbidden is checked
before no-cluster because an RBAC denial mentions the server too.

`--request-timeout` on every call, because kubectl otherwise waits forever
and a dead cluster would hang the exec with no output. The ready column is
rebuilt from container booleans into the `1/2` operators expect, and
restarts report the worst container rather than the first — a pod with one
calm container and one crashlooping is a crashlooping pod.

## Three bugs inherited from the modules written hours earlier

The Docker/cron review landed after this parser was written, and it had all
three of the classes that review found:

- `no such file or directory` in a kubeconfig path error was classified as
  a missing binary — the "go fix the wrong machine" failure. `not-installed`
  is now restricted to shell wordings and checked after the specific cases.
- The section regex required `===\n`, so a CRLF host matched no marker and
  reported an empty cluster. Now `\r?\n`.
- Error-word matching ran over data lines, so a namespace called
  `error-reporting` vanished. Namespaces are now decided by SHAPE — one
  token that is a valid Kubernetes name — which is immune to what anyone
  calls a resource. My first attempt still dropped `unauthorized-probe`,
  because a hyphen is a word boundary; the test caught it.

Also corrects the Docker module description, which advertised "open a shell
inside one" while `buildDockerShellCommand` was wired to nothing. Both the
reviewer and I reached the same conclusion independently: correct the claim
rather than ship an unreviewed exec path to make it true.

22 tests for Kubernetes, including the three inherited classes. 1852
passing, lint and typecheck clean, boots clean.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Add sign out, password reset and Google sign-in

The auth surface was a sign-in form and nothing else.

Sign out: the API had cleared sessions properly since the beginning —
hashed token deleted server-side, cookie cleared — but nothing in the
interface ever called it. The only way out was clearing the cookie by
hand. Now in the sidebar and in the mobile panel, which had no footer
at all.

Password reset: PasswordResetToken stores only a SHA-256 of the value
in the link, for the same reason sessions do. One hour, single use,
and every other session is destroyed on success — if the reset
happened because someone else had the password, leaving their session
alive defeats the point.

The endpoint answers identically whether or not the address has an
account, and every failure — missing, used, expired — returns one
identical message, so a stolen token cannot be probed for which it
was. A 60s per-address cooldown stops it being used to flood an inbox;
it is in-memory and so per-process, and a multi-instance deployment
should move it to Redis.

Email goes through Resend, over fetch and Zod rather than the SDK, as
every other outbound integration here does. Without RESEND_API_KEY the
link is written to the API log instead, and the reset screen says so
rather than promising an inbox — the first version claimed "a reset
link is on its way" when nothing had been sent, which is exactly the
kind of thing the rest of this codebase is careful not to do.

The transport never throws. That looks like sloppiness and is the
requirement: an exception escaping it would hand back the enumeration
signal the endpoint exists to hide. Failures are loud in the log and
invisible to the caller.

Google sign-in: gated on GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/SECRET, and the sign-in page
asks /auth/methods rather than assuming, so an instance without them
renders no button instead of one that dead-ends. Matching is on
Google's `sub` and never on the email address — an address can be
reassigned, and treating it as identity would hand the new owner
someone else's account. It writes UserIdentity rather than
ConnectedAccount: those answer "how do you prove you are you" and
"what do you play on", and merging them would mean disconnecting Steam
could cost you your way back in.

OAuthState.userId becomes nullable, since a sign-in has no session to
attach to yet. The platform-connect path now asserts it is present
rather than assuming.

Phone sign-in is not included. It needs a paid SMS provider account,
and shipping an untested credential-issuing path is worse than
shipping none.

Note: this changes the schema. Run `pnpm --filter @omniplay/database
push` after pulling.

Add component tests, and three bugs they found

61 component tests over the behaviours that fail silently: a focus trap
that has stopped trapping looks identical to one that works unless you
are using a keyboard, a shortcut that fires while you are typing loses
the entry being written, and a form that shows a goal selected and saves
without it looks right until the number is checked weeks later. Several
are regressions that actually happened here.

Three real bugs surfaced while writing them.

The focus trap filtered candidates with `offsetParent !== null`, which is
wrong twice over: it reports null for anything inside a position:fixed
ancestor even when plainly visible, and it depends on layout, so under a
renderer with no layout engine every element looks hidden and the trap
silently became a no-op. Now asks about display and visibility, which
answers the actual question and degrades to "everything is visible"
rather than "nothing is".

The sheet's focus rAF stole focus back from React's autoFocus, so the
composer opened on its first button rather than its amount field, and
anything typed in that frame went to the wrong element. It also never
fired at all in a hidden tab, stranding focus on the body. The DOM is
already mounted when an effect runs, so the frame bought nothing —
focusing synchronously fixes both, and skipping it when the panel already
owns focus leaves autoFocus alone.

The shortcut guard detected contenteditable only through the computed
property, which is not implemented everywhere and misses a target nested
inside the editable host. It now reads the attribute too.

Also: the environment shims needed for jsdom are documented as gaps in
the environment rather than behaviour being faked, and the afterEach hook
always restores real timers — a test that installs fake ones and then
times out never reaches its own cleanup, and every later userEvent call
hangs on a timer nothing will advance.

253 tests.

Fixed the missing argument — and the guard for it immediately found a second one

THE FIX. ep_detector's assemble_judge_inputs(...) call now passes has_direct_source from the
candidate row. One argument, at one call site, missing since the call was written. It is a bug fix
by this file's own precedent (the max_tokens fix: "It WILL change live grades — that is the
point"), shipped on his word because it moves grades.

WHAT WE MISSED IN THE PAST — much less than I feared, and the judge's own rationales say why. I
pulled every routine/MODERATE row of the last 60 days that had a grounded corpus. The judge
repeatedly identified the primary source ITSELF while being told there was none: PRAA "Fresh,
verifiable catalyst exists (8-K/press release dated 2026-08-06)", CRSR "Fresh, primary-sourced
catalyst exists (8-K + press release)", PSIX, TASK, ROCK, CLF, INSP all the same. It read the
evidence instead of trusting the flag. The downgrades it did make rest on substance — SCSC "an 8-K
on a single director's retirement", BRUN "an 8-K announcing the DATE of the Q2 call", SG "only
wrong-company noise about SGX", TEM "~20 days old". So the false "no" cost us little; the fix is
correctness, not recovery.

WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG, which is the part that matters. Nothing fails when a judge is merely
MISINFORMED. No exception, no missing row, no alert — a grade still comes out and every downstream
surface looks healthy. The only thing that could see it was a report that recomputes the truth and
compares, which is the monthly review. That is a thirty-day detection lag on a live-path bug, and

fix: the twenty-first pass's remaining findings (#175)

* fix: secure existing workspace roots, and stop retry racing an orphan

The 0700 workspace fix was partly false and its CHANGELOG entry
overclaimed. mkdir applies a mode only to directories it CREATES, so
every user who ran copy before it kept a 0755 root forever. Measured on
real Linux, before and after. An explicit chmod fixes them, and a root
owned by another uid is now REFUSED rather than copied into: the path is
deterministic inside a shared tmpdir, so on the multi-user machine this
guard exists for, someone else can create it first. Verified in a
container as a non-root user against a root-owned directory.

retryJob refused running/queued to stop two attempts racing one working
directory, and produced exactly that for a derived orphan: its guard
reads the derived status while claimNextJob filters on the raw file,
which still says queued. cancelJob was taught to tell the two kinds of
orphan apart; retry was not. It now marks the original cancelled.

contextJobs dropped jobs past the character budget with no header and no
note, contradicting the contract stated two functions above it. It now
names them. The docblock also claimed oldest entries truncate first,
which was never true of the loop.

The copy path's size refusal named the parent of the project rather than
the workspace, and the force flag's schema description still promised an
unconditional uncommitted-changes refusal that only exists in a git
repo.

* fix: bound the leaderboard body read, and stop leaking MCP sessions

The leaderboard's 8s timeout was cancelled as soon as response headers
arrived, leaving response.json() unbounded -- measured still pending at
15s. Quality scores are awaited per routing candidate, so a half-dead
endpoint stalled every dispatch indefinitely while the class docblock
promised the opposite. Only the placement of clearTimeout changes.

The HTTP server built a per-session McpServer before knowing whether the
request was an initialize. Anything else with an unknown session id is
answered 400 without initialising, so neither onsessioninitialized nor
onclose ever fired and the server stayed resident: five such requests,
five orphans. Sessions were also never expired -- the SDK closes one
only on an explicit HTTP DELETE, which the standard client never sends,
so a clean client shutdown left its session forever. They now idle out
after 30 minutes, swept on request rather than on a timer.

openMcpSessions() is exposed on the handle because the leak is otherwise
unobservable; a test reimplementing the bookkeeping would pin its own
copy rather than this one.

subscriptions.name: HARTOS
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(session): stop boot-time inference starving the compositor's first paint

The native compositor (hart-comp) sometimes lost its first-paint race and got
HANG-dropped to the sway fallback tier. Root cause found live on .69
(2026-09-02): hart-llm's ~68s model-load warmup and hart-agent-daemon's
autonomous goal dispatch are both only `wantedBy hart.target` with NO ordering
against the session, so on a cold boot they run INSIDE hart-comp's
shellPaintTimeoutSeconds (120s) window and push first paint past it. The
supervisor then drops native to sway. The one fresh-boot re-promotion
(session-tier.hang) recovers native — but only on the NEXT boot: measured boot 1
dropped to sway under a llama-load + dispatch burst, boot 2 latched hart-comp on
the byte-identical compositor binary. For a latency-first appliance native must
latch on the FIRST boot.

Add hart-await-first-paint: a oneshot ordered `before` hart-llm and
hart-agent-daemon that waits for the session's shell-ready marker (touched by
WHICHEVER tier paints) before releasing them, so first paint runs unstarved. It
is pure ordering — greetd depends on neither it nor hart-llm, so no cycle; it is
not required/wanted BY its consumers, so a failure can't wedge them; and it is
bounded to the paint budget + margin, after which inference is released
regardless (a genuinely non-painting session is the supervisor's own drop-path
problem). Defined in the supervisor module, which OWNS shell-ready and is enabled
only where a compositor exists — server/edge keep starting inference immediately.
One gate for both services: no per-service duplication.

Does NOT touch the compositor binary, the paint watchdog, or the drop/re-promote
logic — the freeze-detection safety net is unchanged; this only removes the
contention that was tripping it. tests/unit/test_nixos_configs.py pins the
ordering (before both services, ordering-only, bounded, canonical marker).

deploy: a fresh clone has no book.sexp, and the build assumed one

The first deploy on a clean droplet failed in its first second, at the last
COPY in the Dockerfile: book.sexp is gitignored -- it is the owner's private
book -- so a clone does not contain it, and BuildKit refuses the build while
computing cache keys, before a line of OCaml compiles. The local harness could

deploy-verify` was green against a context the droplet does not have.

now say what is actually committed: the example.

book.example.sexp as the baked-in fallback, since that file exists in every
checkout. deploy.sh creates book.sexp from the example when absent -- and
this one matters beyond the build, because the compose file bind-mounts
../book.sexp into both engines, and Docker's response to a missing bind-mount
source is to create it as a directory, which mounted over a file fails the
container with an error that names neither. An existing book.sexp is never

feat(widget): handlers on the remaining interactive widgets

Extends what Button, Checkbox, TextInput and Slider already had to
List::on_select, Select::on_select, Tabs::on_select, Table::on_select,
TextArea::on_input, Splitter::on_change, Toolbar::on_item, Menu::on_item and
Radio::on_select. Each is bound to the action that widget's ontology
advertises, so an application driven by any of them writes no execute_action
handler.

Doing this surfaced a defect in the previous commit. Checkbox advertises
`toggle` in its ontology, but its handler was registered under `click`: an
agent reading the ontology would call the name the widget published and
nothing would happen. Three tests passed only because they called `click`
directly, encoding the bug rather than catching it.

Fixed three ways. Handlers bind to the advertised action. A mouse click fires
whichever action the widget registered, since a click means "activate this",
not any particular name. And validate now reports `unadvertised_action` when
a handler answers something its widget does not publish, so the class of
fault cannot recur silently -- the library's own widgets are asserted clean
by that check.

A sweep test drives all five newly handled widget kinds through the protocol
and asserts each change reached the model, because compiling is not evidence
that a handler is reachable.

fabrication-resistance must be a property of STRUCTURE, not discipline; the
best-railed agent in that fleet is railed by a machine contract that bounces

Permit-null is named as the actual anti-sycophancy primitive: an agent that can

where a candidate becomes a claim); a cooperative Falsify stage produces

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(daemon): stop away-mode busy-guard false positives and refuse silent wedge-alarm entry (#2)

* fix: stop away-mode's busy guard from wedging on settled scrollback

Two real away-mode sessions delivered zero escalations for 2+ hours each
because pane_is_busy() misread the captain's idle pane as busy on every
15s cycle. Live measurement in an isolated Herdr lab disproved the
suspected cause (the daemon's own tracked background job wedging its
hosting pane): a real fm-supervise-daemon.sh, launched exactly as
production does and targeting its own hosting pane, delivered a seeded
escalation successfully with a background shell alive the whole time.

The actual cause: pane_is_busy's rendered-tail fallback has no positional
anchor. Claude's busy-shape signature ("…" + a parenthesized elapsed
duration) is meant to catch a live spinner footer, but it matches equally
well against ordinary SETTLED reply text sitting in scrollback (e.g. "...
holding steady… (2h into the soak test)"). With no new output landing
while escalations keep failing, nothing scrolls the line out of view, so
the false match persists for the rest of the session - reproduced live
and confirmed as the trigger.

Fix: pane_is_busy now treats an affirmatively empty composer as positive
proof the turn has ended and short-circuits the rendered scan before it
runs. A genuinely busy pane never reads an empty composer, so this can't
mask a real busy turn. Both the terminal-backed and native-hosted launch
paths share this same check, so neither needed separate handling.

Separately, the wedge alarm's own escape hatch was inert on this Linux
box: no osascript, no org.freedesktop.Notifications D-Bus service, and
even herdr's own notification channel reported {"reason":"disabled"}
rather than posting anything. Extracted the channel-resolution logic into
bin/fm-wedge-alarm-lib.sh (shared by the daemon and the launcher) and
added an entry-time refusal: fm-afk-launch.sh now refuses a fresh away-mode
entry when no channel can plausibly reach the captain, unless the captain
has explicitly configured one (including an explicit "off" acknowledging
marker-only).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019924TgGwpoBc2rKMbFgi67

* no-mistakes(review): Fix wedge-alarm rollback test, validate directives, add preflight tests

* no-mistakes(document): docs: note directive validation and list fm-wedge-alarm-lib.sh in toolbelt

* no-mistakes(lint): {"summary": "suppress false-positive SC2016 in wedge-alarm preflight test"}

* fix: reject a bare command: wedge-alarm directive at entry

wedge_alarm_reliable_channel_configured matched command:* as a reliable
directive even with an empty payload, so a config/wedge-alarm containing
only "command:" passed away-mode entry as covered while
wedge_alarm_via_command's own non-empty-cmd guard silently no-ops it at
alarm time - the exact reassurance-that-doesn't-hold gap this predicate
exists to catch. Require at least one character after the colon
(command:?*) so an empty payload falls into the same immediate rejection
as any other unrecognized directive.

osascript and herdr are left unchanged: a missing binary is a per-host
environmental fact, the same class of runtime risk this predicate already
leaves to wedge_alarm_notify's best-effort logged dispatch for a broken
command:<cmd> payload, not a config-only defect like an empty command:.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LnXRSBGuVx1oZEnPdKxm8F

* no-mistakes(ci): Fixed the Greptile-flagged gap in bin/fm-wedge-alarm-lib.sh: `wedge_alarm_reliable_channel_configured` used the case pattern `command:?*`, which requires only one character after the colon — so `command: ` (or any all-whitespace payload) matched and was accepted as a "reliable" channel at away-mode entry. At runtime, `wedge_alarm_via_command`'s `[ -n "$cmd" ]` guard treats whitespace as non-empty too, so `sh -c ' '` would run, do nothing, and exit 0 — silently no-op'ing the alarm with no signal to the captain, reproducing the exact fail-silent gap this PR's user intent targets. Fix: changed the pattern to `command:*[![:space:]]*`, requiring at least one non-whitespace character after the colon, so both a bare `command:` and a whitespace-only `command: ` are rejected at entry (falling into the existing "no active wedge-alarm channel is configured" refusal), while `command:<real cmd>` still passes. Updated the adjacent comment to document the whitespace case. Added a regression test (`unit_wedge_alarm_preflight_refuses_whitespace_command_directive` in tests/fm-afk-launch.test.sh) that pins FM_WEDGE_ALARM_CHANNEL='command: ' being rejected; verified it fails on the pre-fix code and passes after the fix. Confirmed the CI/CD runs for this PR are conclusion=action_required (workflow-approval gating, not a real test failure), so the only concrete code defect to address was the Greptile finding. Full fm-afk-launch.test.sh and fm-daemon.test.sh suites pass (all wedge-alarm preflight + dispatch tests green), and shellcheck is clean on both changed files

Remove the Discord references, and gate their absence

No Discord integration or credential was ever in this repo — the presence MCP
was excluded before the first commit, the live MCP set is playwright, context7
and t3mp3st, and `git log -S` finds no Discord secret in any commit. What
remained were five cosmetic mentions of discord.com as one of the sampled
design systems in the third-party design-extract gallery.

- library/build-index.mjs gains an EXCLUDE list, applied when rows are
  collected. INDEX.md is generated from a library that is re-cloned per
  machine, so hand-editing it would have been undone by the next regeneration;
  excluding at the source is what makes the omission survive one.
- The gallery's example lists in config/ui-design-stack.md, library/sources.json
  and skills/design-tokens/SKILL.md drop it. Counts follow: 24 indexed design
  systems become 23, and the index falls from 815 skills to 814. `linear` was
  wrong as a replacement example — it has a gallery directory but no token
  skill — so the lists name raycast instead.
- tools/test/excluded-vendors.test.mjs is the gate. Absence is exactly the kind
  of property that rots silently, so it is now checked: no tracked file may name
  an excluded vendor except the two whose job is to exclude or detect it, and a
  second test asserts those two still do, so a stale exemption cannot keep the
  gate passing over a deleted filter. Proven to have teeth against a control.

Two references remain, both deliberate: the EXCLUDE entry that keeps the name
out of the index, and the scan-secrets.mjs pattern that catches a Discord bot
token before it can be committed. A scanner that cannot name what it found is
decoration, and removing that pattern would weaken the protection the rest of
this change exists to provide.

Verified: root 150/150 and argo 440/440 on Node 24.19 and Node 20.20; doctor
31 ok; scan-secrets clean; sync --check 0 drifted.

feat(vpn): boot/daemon guard unit for reattach coverage

vpn_reattach_guard runs only when the script runs. A reboot or a docker daemon
restart brings containers back by restart-policy WITHOUT the script, so a
gluetun recreated on boot could orphan its borrowers with nothing to catch it
until the next manual up/update. Add mediastack-vpnguard.service (oneshot,
After/Requires=docker.service, WantedBy=multi-user.target) running a new
'vpn-guard --boot' subcommand on every boot and docker restart.

The subcommand waits (bounded 120s, mirroring cmd_up) for gluetun to become
healthy before judging attachment — at boot, docker starts containers
asynchronously, so checking too early would race the startup it guards and
false-repair. If gluetun is absent on boot (stack not meant to be up) it
no-ops; run by hand with no gluetun it dies loudly. The unit is installed and
refreshed idempotently by cmd_up (removed unit reappears next up; daemon-reload
only when the file actually changes), and both uninstall paths remove it.

Closes the boot/daemon drift window. Does NOT cover raw out-of-band
'docker compose up' mid-session — that remains the reattach guard's job on the
next script invocation, or a future topological (internal-network) fix.
